\section[el divorcio]{el divorcio — the divorce}

\label{lesson:ES-C550-divorcio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the husband, then the Spanish for to toast.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el divorcio}
\textbf{el divorcio} — \textquotedblleft{}the divorce\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El divorcio fue difícil para los niños.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The divorce was hard for the children.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{divorcio} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{dīvortium} 'a separation, a divorce' (EtymDB), built on \emph{dīvertere} 'to turn aside'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el divorcio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el divorcio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el divorcio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the husband, then the Spanish for to toast, then say \emph{el divorcio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el divorcio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The divorce\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[separarse]{separarse — to separate, to split up}

\label{lesson:ES-C550-separarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to toast, then the Spanish for the divorce.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: separarse}
\textbf{separarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to separate, to split up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se separaron después de diez años.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They split up after ten years.}
\end{quote}

Without \emph{se}: \emph{separar} is to separate two things.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{separarse} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{sēparāre} 'to set apart' (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{sē-} 'apart' and \emph{parāre} 'to make ready'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{separarse}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{separarse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{separarse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to toast, then the Spanish for the divorce, then say \emph{separarse} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does separarse mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To separate, to split up\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[divorciado]{divorciado — divorced}

\label{lesson:ES-C550-divorciado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the divorce, then the Spanish for to separate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: divorciado}
\textbf{divorciado} — \textquotedblleft{}divorced\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Está divorciado y tiene dos hijos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He is divorced and has two children.}
\end{quote}

Used with \emph{estar}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{divorciado} is built on the participle of \emph{divorciar}, from \emph{divorcio}, a learned word from Latin \emph{dīvortium} 'a separation' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{divorciado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{divorciado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the divorce, then the Spanish for to separate, then say \emph{divorciado} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does divorciado mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Divorced\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el viudo]{el viudo — the widower; widowed}

\label{lesson:ES-C550-viudo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to separate, then the Spanish for divorced.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el viudo}
\textbf{el viudo} — \textquotedblleft{}the widower; widowed\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi abuelo es viudo desde hace años.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My grandfather has been a widower for years.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Quedarse viudo} — to be widowed.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{viudo} is inherited from Latin \emph{viduus} 'bereaved, widowed' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la viuda]{la viuda — the widow}

\label{lesson:ES-C550-viuda}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for divorced, then the Spanish for the widower.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la viuda}
\textbf{la viuda} — \textquotedblleft{}the widow\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La viuda vive sola en el pueblo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The widow lives alone in the village.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{viuda} is inherited from Latin \emph{vidua} 'a widow' (EtymDB), the feminine of \emph{viduus} 'bereaved'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
